noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: know and be able to explain the shapes of, and bond angles in, BeCl 2 , BCl 3 , CH 4 , NH 3 , NH + , H O, CO , gaseous PCl , SF and C H 4 2 2 5 6 2 4

primer.text: Molecules are shaped by mutual repulsion: electron pairs around a central atom spread as far apart as possible, with lone pairs pressing hardest, and bond length falling as attraction rises - triple bonds shortest and strongest. This note assembles the VSEPR rules, the repulsion ladder, the length-strength coupling and the catalogue of shapes with their signature angles.

lessons.title: Repulsion as the architect
lessons.opening: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory predicts molecular shapes from one principle: electrons repel. Bonding pairs around a central atom push each other apart until the molecule settles into the arrangement that minimises those forces. The rule stack has fine print - lone pairs repel hardest, multiple bonds count differently - and the repulsion ladder runs lone-lone above lone-bond above bond-bond.
keyPoints: VSEPR's job is predicting molecular shapes together with their bond angles.
Electron pairs repel because they carry the same negative charge.
Molecules adopt the shape that minimises the repulsive forces around the central atom.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonded pairs - their charge clouds are more concentrated and sit closer to the nucleus.
Repulsion strength descends: two lone pairs first, a lone pair against a bond pair next, two bond pairs last.

low.restatement: Count the electron clouds around the central atom and spread them as far apart as possible - that spread is the molecular shape.
low.analogy: Balloons tied to one point shove each other into the most even spread the strings allow - the balloon bundle is the molecule.
low.examPointer: When justifying a shape, open with 'electron pairs repel to minimise repulsion' - it is the theory in one line.

medium.restatement: VSEPR treats each electron domain as a repulsive agent whose strength varies by type: lone pairs, held by one nucleus, carry wider, denser clouds that press harder than bonds shared between two nuclei, so the geometry settles where total repulsion is least.
medium.analogy: Occupants of a shared office: the solo occupant with the biggest luggage (lone pair) claims extra floor space, squeezing the paired colleagues closer together.
medium.examPointer: Ranking questions want the full ladder - lone-lone, lone-bond, bond-bond - in order, with the concentrated-cloud reason attached.

check.stem: What does VSEPR theory predict?

options.text: The shapes and bond angles of molecules
options.explanation: Repulsion minimisation fixes the geometry.
Colour lies outside VSEPR's remit.
Mass is irrelevant to the repulsion model.
Kinetics is a different theory.

check.stem: Why do electron pairs repel each other?

options.text: They carry the same negative charge
options.explanation: Like charges push apart.

options.text: They attract each other too strongly
options.explanation: Repulsion, not attraction, drives the geometry.

options.text: Nuclei pull them into each other
options.explanation: Nuclei anchor pairs; the pairs push apart.

options.text: They have no charge at all
options.explanation: Their charge is the cause.

check.stem: Which pair combination repels most strongly?

options.explanation: The concentrated clouds press hardest.
That is the weakest repulsion of the three.
Intermediate strength.
The three strengths differ measurably.

check.stem: Why do lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs?

options.text: Their charge cloud is more concentrated and sits closer to the central nucleus
options.explanation: Held by one nucleus instead of two, the cloud spreads wider near the atom.
A lone pair is still one negative pair.
Spin plays no role here.

options.text: They are further from the nucleus
options.explanation: They sit closer, not further.

check.stem: How is the repulsion between a double bond and a single bond treated in VSEPR?

options.text: The same as repulsion between two single bonds
options.explanation: One double bond counts as one domain against a single.
The rule of record treats them the same.
No halving rule exists.

options.text: Repulsion does not apply to multiple bonds
options.explanation: Multiple bonds still repel.

check.stem: State what VSEPR stands for and what it predicts.
check.modelAnswer: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, which predicts the shapes and bond angles of molecules.

check.stem: State the repulsion order for lone and bonding pairs.
check.modelAnswer: Strongest first: lone-with-lone, then lone-against-bond, then bond-with-bond.

check.stem: Explain why a molecule adopts the shape it does, in VSEPR terms.
check.modelAnswer: The electron pairs around the central atom all repel each other, so the molecule settles into the arrangement that pushes those clouds as far apart as possible - the geometry with the least total repulsion is the stable one.

check.stem: Predict whether replacing a bonding pair with a lone pair on a central atom increases or decreases the pressure on the remaining bonds, and why.
check.modelAnswer: It increases the pressure: the lone pair's more concentrated cloud repels harder than the bond pair it replaced, squeezing the remaining bonds closer together.

lessons.title: Bond length pays for strength
lessons.opening: Bond length is simply the internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms. Stronger attraction between the shared electrons and the two nuclei pulls the atoms closer - shortening the bond and strengthening it in the same stroke. Triple bonds show the effect at its limit: their dense electron clouds draw the nuclei nearest, making them the shortest and strongest covalent bonds.
keyPoints: Bond length is the internuclear distance of two covalently bonded atoms.
Greater attraction between electrons and nuclei pulls the atoms closer together.
Shorter bond length goes with stronger covalent bonding.
The triple bond tops both charts - shortest in length, strongest in hold.
Their large electron density between the nuclei raises the attraction and shortens the distance.

low.restatement: The more strongly the electrons glue two nuclei together, the closer those nuclei sit - and the closer they sit, the harder the bond resists breaking.
low.analogy: Two magnets pulled together by stronger grip end up nearer and harder to separate: strength and closeness are one outcome.
low.examPointer: The pairing 'shorter and stronger' must travel together in answers - quoting only half loses the mark.

medium.restatement: Bond length is the electrostatic equilibrium distance: electron density concentrated between the nuclei raises the attractive force per unit distance, so the equilibrium slides inward; bond order raises that density, hence triple bonds sit shortest and strongest.
medium.analogy: A tighter hammock sag: more fabric tension (electron density) pulls both posts (nuclei) inward and makes the setup harder to snap.
medium.examPointer: Order the bonds by length and strength together: single longest and weakest, triple shortest and strongest.

check.stem: What is bond length?

options.text: The internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms
options.explanation: Nucleus to nucleus across the bond.

options.text: The radius of the larger atom
options.explanation: That is an atomic property, not a bond property.

options.text: The distance between two electron pairs
options.explanation: Electron pairs are not the reference points.

options.text: The vibration amplitude of a bond
options.explanation: Vibration is motion, not the equilibrium distance.

check.stem: What happens to bond length when attraction between electrons and nuclei increases?

options.text: The atoms pull closer, decreasing the bond length
options.explanation: Stronger grip shortens the distance.

options.text: The atoms drift apart, increasing bond length
options.explanation: The grip does the opposite.
Length responds to the attraction strength.
Stronger attraction stabilises, not breaks.

check.stem: Which bond type is both the shortest and the strongest?

options.explanation: Maximum electron density pulls hardest and nearest.
Singles are the longest and weakest.
Intermediate on both counts.

options.text: All bond types match in length
options.explanation: Length varies systematically with bond order.

check.stem: Why do triple bonds achieve the shortest length?

options.text: Their large electron density between the nuclei increases the attractive forces
options.explanation: More shared density pulls the nuclei nearer.
The atoms are unchanged; the sharing density is what grows.
Triple bonds add shared pairs, none removed.

options.text: Their bonds are made of stronger atoms
options.explanation: Element identity is fixed in the comparison.

check.stem: Increasing the strength of a covalent bond by pulling its atoms closer has what combined effect?

options.text: Bond length decreases and bond strength increases
options.explanation: The two movements are one event.

options.text: Bond length increases and strength decreases
options.explanation: That inverts both.
The movements cannot decouple that way here.
The coupling is the lesson of the note.

check.stem: Define bond length.
check.modelAnswer: Bond length is the internuclear distance of two covalently bonded atoms.

check.stem: State which bond type is shortest and strongest, with the reason.
check.modelAnswer: Triple bonds - their large electron density between the nuclei raises attraction, pulling the atoms closest.

check.stem: Explain why greater electron-nucleus attraction strengthens a covalent bond.
check.modelAnswer: Stronger attraction holds the shared electrons more firmly between the two nuclei and draws those nuclei nearer, so more energy is required to separate the bonded atoms - which is precisely a stronger bond.

check.stem: Arrange single, double and triple bonds by increasing bond length and state the strength order that accompanies it.
check.modelAnswer: Length: triple < double < single; strength runs the same ladder upward - triple strongest, single weakest - because density between the nuclei rises with bond order.

lessons.title: The shape and angle catalogue
lessons.opening: Once repulsion sets the geometry, each molecular shape carries its own signature bond angle: straight lines at 180 degrees, flat triangles at 120, tetrahedra at 109.5. The catalogue of shapes - linear through to bipyramidal - is the working vocabulary VSEPR hands the chemist, and matching a molecule to its entry is the daily exam task.
keyPoints: Molecules adopt characteristic shapes, each with its corresponding bond angles.
Linear molecules carry 180 degree bond angles.
Trigonal planar molecules carry 120 degree angles.
Matching a molecule to its catalogue shape-and-angle entry is the standard VSEPR exercise.

low.restatement: Each molecular shape has a built-in angle: straight (180), flat triangle (120), pyramid corners (109.5) - learn the catalogue and the shapes come with their angles attached.
low.analogy: A set of folding chairs: each design opens to its own fixed angle, and naming the design names the angle.
low.examPointer: Quote angles with the degree sign and the shape name together - 'tetrahedral, 109.5' - neither half alone scores full marks.

medium.restatement: The angle follows from the repulsion geometry: two domains spread to 180, three to 120, four to 109.5 - and lone-pair pressure deviates the catalogue values downward, which is why angles are diagnostic of the domain arrangement underneath.
medium.analogy: Equal spokes on a wheel space at fixed angles; swap one spoke for a wider hub (lone pair) and the remaining spokes lean a little closer.
medium.examPointer: The three anchor angles - 180, 120, 109.5 - cover most exam molecules; anchor them before adding the deviant cases.

check.stem: Which bond angle belongs to a linear molecule?

options.explanation: Two domains spread to opposite directions.
That is the trigonal planar angle.
That is the tetrahedral angle.
Bipyramidal geometry uses 90, not linear.

check.stem: Which molecular shape carries 120 degree bond angles?

options.explanation: Three domains spread in one plane.
Linear runs at 180.
Tetrahedral runs at 109.5.
Pyramidal shapes deviate below 109.5.

check.stem: The tetrahedral bond angle is

options.explanation: Four equal domains spread into 3D.
That is the planar value.
That is the linear value.
That appears in bipyramidal arrangements.

check.stem: Why do the catalogue angles differ between shapes?

options.text: Different numbers of electron domains spread by different minimum-repulsion geometry
options.explanation: More domains crowd into 3D space with smaller separations.
The values are systematic.
Mass plays no role.

options.text: Angles depend on colour and state
options.explanation: Neither enters the geometry.

check.stem: Two molecules both carry four electron domains. Their bond angles should be

options.text: approximately equal, at the tetrahedral value
options.explanation: Matching domain counts give matching base geometry.
Domain count drives the base angle.
Four domains never settle to 180.
VSEPR exists precisely to predict this.

check.stem: State the bond angles of linear, trigonal planar and tetrahedral shapes.
check.modelAnswer: Linear 180 degrees, trigonal planar 120 degrees, tetrahedral 109.5 degrees.

check.stem: State what VSEPR pairs with every molecular shape it names.
check.modelAnswer: Each shape carries its corresponding bond angles - the catalogue pairs shape with angle.

check.stem: Explain why four electron domains settle at 109.5 degrees rather than 120.
check.modelAnswer: Four clouds cannot fit in one plane; they spread into three dimensions, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron whose interior angles - 109.5 degrees - minimise the mutual repulsion.

check.stem: A molecule shows three electron domains around its central atom. Predict its shape and bond angle via the catalogue.
check.modelAnswer: Three domains spread in one plane: trigonal planar shape with 120 degree bond angles.

glossary.definition: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, predicting molecular shapes and angles from electron-pair repulsion.
A pair of valence electrons held by one atom that do not bond, repelling more strongly than bonding pairs.
The internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms.
The angle between two bonds sharing a central atom, fixed by the repulsion geometry.
